children: With the conversations of Day 1 setting the tone for what lies ahead, the BW Hotelier Indian Hospitality Summit & Awards (IHA 2026) returned for its second day at the JW Marriott New Delhi Aerocity. The opening day brought together hospitality leaders, developers, investors, global brands and industry veterans, with discussions spanning growth, capital, development, leadership and the changing business of hospitality. Day 2 picked up from where those conversations left off, bringing a fresh set of voices and perspectives to the table.
Under the theme ‘Growth Engines’, Day 2 turned the spotlight to the forces that will drive India’s hospitality industry through its next phase. The session titled,
“Can Hospitality Become India's Career of Choice? Winning the Talent Battle”,
brought together senior human resources and people leaders to discuss the sector’s talent priorities.

The discussion was chaired by Yateendra Sinh, Principal, YS & Associates, Sàrl, Switzerland, and brought together Vinay Jaswal, VP, HR Operations (South Asia), Marriott International; Nilesh Mitra, VP, Talent Management, ITC Hotels Limited; Amit Malik, VP - People & Culture, South Asia, Accor; Mehr Sanduja, Director - People & Culture South Asia, Radisson Hotel Group; Mielle Batliwala, VP - Human Resources, Sarovar Hotels; and Rohit Pandey, VP, Human Resources, The Leela Palaces, Hotels and Resorts.

Pandey said, “The Leela has been the aspirational brand leader in the industry when it comes to talent. I would want to explore every avenue to find the right talent, and we want to attract talent from beyond the traditional IHMs”.“This year at The Leela, we have reached out to almost 80 colleges that are not IHMs. We want to expand our talent pool and explore institutions beyond the traditional hospitality education ecosystem to find the right talent,” he added.

Malik said, “Technology signals innovation when it comes to recruitment. There is a lot of talent that hospitality industry graduates bring to the industry and contribute to the overall economy as well.” “Parents have a great influence on the career choices their wards make. This is an important factor when we look at how young talent makes decisions about their careers and the opportunities they choose,” Malik added.“We are providing leadership experiences through initiatives that allow young talent to experience work-life balance and pursue the things they want alongside their careers. We are focussed on creating experiences that make hospitality careers more relevant to the next generation,” he added.

“The industry has emotional anchors, which happen around purpose and prestige. These emotional connections are important when it comes to attracting and engaging the next generation of talent,” said Nilesh Mitra.“There was visible mentorship on the floor, and conversations with leaders were meant to inspire, not enquire. Creating those interactions and giving young talent the opportunity to engage with leaders can make a difference in how they perceive the industry,” he added.

Vinay Jaswal elaborated , “Principally, the question should change from why people are not joining us to what we are doing to make people join us. We need to look at how we can make the industry and the opportunities within it more attractive to the next generation.” “We, at Marriott, are focussed on providing experiences to the next generation.

We have interwoven career pathways across multiple segments, giving young talent the opportunity to explore different roles and build their careers within the organisation,” he explained. “We all admit that in the last decade, and especially after Covid, the hospitality industry has gone through a massive change. The expectations of talent have changed, and the industry needs to respond to those changing expectations,” Jaswal added.

Sanduja addressed, “We need to understand what talent requires from the industry. Just a monthly activity or a birthday bash is not enough to engage and retain talent. We need to look beyond routine engagement activities and understand what truly matters to our people. The focus should be on creating meaningful experiences, understanding their expectations and building an environment where they feel valued and connected to the organisation. With 20 openings planned in a year, we are looking to hire approximately 100 employees for each hotel.       ”

Batliwala elaborated, “We need to stop looking at hospitality purely through the lens of luxury. If there’s something that adds value to their learning, they will have a reason to stay with a brand for longer. When the younger generation knows that an organisation is invested in their growth and learning, they will stay longer. We are in the process of transitioning our learning system, and when we surveyed the company, we learnt that no one wants classroom training; they prefer hands-on learning. One of the biggest reasons people love working with us is that they get to work close to home. We are spread across more than 90 locations in India today, and we will need about 3,000–3,500 people over the next four years,”

As the conversation drew to a close, the panel stressed that solving the industry's staffing bottleneck requires more than just better recruitment pitches. By tackling long-standing issues around compensation, work-life balance, and continuous learning, hotel groups can build an environment where young professionals feel valued, supported, and motivated to build lifelong careers in hospitality.

The conversations will eventually give way to celebration as IHA 2026 heads into its Gala Awards evening. As the two-day gathering comes to a close, BW Hotelier will recognise accomplished hoteliers and hospitality organisations across 20+ categories, acknowledging the people and businesses that have driven the sector’s growth and evolution.
